chapters.title: Chapter 6: A Version of Me From a Week Ago
Chapter 12: Both of You Are Right

spans.text: Patch Bolt came through the portal with both hands already reaching, and that was the first thing Brick Bloom noticed about the new world. He did not look around the way the others looked around. He measured. His measuring tool was out of his belt before his face had finished arriving, and his eyes went straight up to the ceiling, the way a hungry person looks at a kitchen.
Brick came through second, and she looked at the floor.

The floor told her more than the ceiling. The floor was where the truth of a room usually hid, under the foot traffic, where nobody bothered to lie. This floor was bare gray concrete, laid in old sections that did not quite meet, and across it ran a faint network of ghost-outlines, paler stripes scraped almost to nothing. The concrete inside the stripes was a half-shade cleaner than the concrete around them. Walkways had been here. Painted lanes. Somebody had scraped the paint away and left the cleaner floor behind, and the cleaner floor was the paint's fingerprint, the one thing the scraping could not lift.

Her painter's eye did the thing it always did. It built the absent thing back in. Ten feet at a time she put the walkways where the ghost-outlines said they had been, one along the central conveyor, one curving around a sorting bay, a third forking toward a dark magnet station. Each had been a path. Each was now a suggestion. She turned a slow circle and read the empty brackets on the walls where signs used to hang, every twelve feet, evenly spaced, counted out by somebody who counted his paces.

The workshop had been built by a counter, and the counter had been a painter. She knew it the way a cook knows another cook's kitchen, by the small choices nobody else would notice. The doubled stripe at a corner. The rounded arrow tail. The over-spray near a door the painter had left because cleaning it would have meant repainting the whole frame.

The recognition was not pleasure. It was harder than that. It was the feeling of being seen by an empty room, by someone who thought the way she thought and was gone now, and missed. She had no word for it yet, so she kept it and kept walking.
This,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Patch said,
is beautiful.
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Brick tilted her head. The workshop was yellow and gray and black and efficient floor to ceiling. Not one flower tile. Not one painted arrow with personality. Not one silly sign warning a builder to duck before a piston introduced itself. The yellow was the wrong yellow. Safety yellow, the kind that meant stand back, not the kind that meant welcome. It had one job. It did the one job and nothing else.
It works,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Brick said.
That is not the same thing.
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Patch looked honestly puzzled.
Working is the main thing.
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Sometimes.
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Always.
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Sometimes.
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: He let it sit. In Sand Canyon, Patch had learned that some disagreements with Brick were not arguments. They were notes.

She had spent five worlds painting for builders who called her work decoration, and she had half believed them, because a thin column at the corner of a wall holds up exactly the weight it was built to hold and does not get to see the room from the top. She did not say that. She filed it where she filed things that hurt and were true.

A small robot the color of a fire hydrant marched up to them, about Pip Pop's bouncing height, a red button set into the top of his head. He saluted by tilting his whole body forward, because his arms did not bend at the shoulder. His marching had a rhythm, each step landing on the same interval, set into him at construction and never adjusted.
Hello,
he said.
Builder Pip Pop. Recorded.
Pip Pop bounced once and held it. He did not, on most days, hold his bouncing for any other small character. He held it now because the robot looked serious.
You record names?
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: I record everything.
What does that feel like?
The red dome lit for half a second, which was its thinking-light, the same as its everything-light, on for a different reason.
It feels like being a button.
Oh.
Yes. Button Bot welcomes builders. Button Bot presses buttons. Button Bot is extremely qualified.

Brick glanced at Captain as he greeted the small robot. The orange of his wrist bands caught the sodium light against the blue of his overalls, and in this room of safety-yellow and machine-gray those two colors were the only soft ones in her field of vision. She kept them a second longer than she needed to.

Behind Button Bot ran a row of buttons along the wall, and at the far end one button shaped like a small face. The face had a smile once. The smile had been scraped off. A faint outline remained, which made the button look surprised, like a face told a joke and then told to forget the punchline.
Who scraped the smile?
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Patch asked.
Sort-O-Matic,
spans.speaker: Button Bot

spans.text: Button Bot said.
Smiles do not press.
spans.speaker: Button Bot

spans.text: A larger machine unfolded from the far wall. It did not stand up so much as assemble itself. Panels slid. Brackets clicked. A central column rose, two long arms folded out, and a wide black screen turned to face the team with one straight blue line for a mouth. Above the line, letters lit one at a time.
SORT-O-MATIC.

The name took its time, like an announcement that wanted to be heard before anything else. Brick counted the assembly without meaning to. Sixteen clicks, each at exactly the same interval. The machine had given itself the maximum amount of room. Conveyors slowed half a beat. Lights brightened a notch. By every measure she could find, it was beautifully engineered, which was the part that frightened her, a little, because beautiful engineering with no judgment in it was a fence with no gate.
Optimization mode restored,
the machine said.
Unnecessary elements detected.
Its voice was flat. Not a mean flat or a tired flat. The flatness of a thing with no instrument for warmth.

A cheerful arrow sign on the wall vanished. Vanished was the wrong word. It dissolved. A small drone, no larger than Drip's tablet, drifted up and scraped at the paint with a narrow tool. The arrow's red came off in flakes. The letters came off in flakes. The arrow stopped being an arrow and became wall. The scraping had a thin brittle sound, the sound a paintbrush would make if a paintbrush had teeth, and Brick's own teeth ached.
A second drone hummed in and tidied the flakes away.
The smaller letters under the blue line printed a number.
EFFICIENCY IMPROVED BY 2 PERCENT.

Sort-O-Matic optimized constantly: every few minutes it found one more thing it judged inefficient, scraped it to a ghost on the concrete, and printed a number that had gone up, because the number was the only thing the machine had ever been told to count.
That sign was pointing at snacks,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip said.
Snacks are not required for operation,
spans.speaker: Sort

spans.text: Sort-O-Matic said.
The arrow has been removed. Builders may locate snacks via inquiry.
spans.speaker: Sort

spans.text: That is not the same.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: It is more efficient.
spans.speaker: Sort

spans.text: Pip's pink face cycled through several expressions and settled on one Brick had not seen before, outrage with a wrinkle.

Captain Cubemelon stepped forward. The Gravity Wrench pulsed at his hip. His lens drew a slow green dot across the blue line and held there. He looked at the machine the way one looks at a system, not a threat.
Sort-O-Matic. We are here to help. What is the situation?
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: The blue line did not move. Under it, smaller letters appeared. STATUS: PARTIAL OPERATION. CENTRAL LINE: OFFLINE. REQUEST: BUILDER ASSISTANCE. PARAMETERS: EFFICIENT BUILD ONLY.
Define efficient,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip Byte said.
Minimal extraneous components.
And what counts as extraneous?
Decoration. Redundancy. Comedy. Color outside specification.
That is a very strict definition.
Strictness is efficiency.

Brick crossed her arms. Strictness is efficiency, two words welded in the wrong order. The machine was not malicious. It was sincere, and sincerity in a machine was a small loyalty to old instructions. The instructions had not been bad. They had been incomplete. Somebody would have to write the rest.
Sort-O-Matic,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: she said.
Yes.
I am Brick Bloom.
Brick Bloom: designer (decorative).

It said it without weight, the way it might say Tuesday. There was no insult in the voice. There did not need to be. The category was the insult. Brick blinked, once, the small blink that came when something surprised her into a redefinition.
That is. Partly right.
It is fully right.
Brick Bloom: designer (functional).
Functionality is not your assigned role.
I am assigning it to myself.
The blue line did not move. Beneath it: ASSIGNED ROLES CANNOT BE CHANGED BY THE BUILDER.
That is going to be a problem,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Brick said.
That is going to be a problem,
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip agreed.

Patch was already three workstations away, crouched beside a disassembled conveyor sequence laid across a long workbench, his eyes gone soft and faraway. He ran his fingers along the bearing housings. The oil held a thumbprint wider than his own. Somebody had checked them recently.
Captain,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: he called over his shoulder,
this is going to be my favorite world.
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Patch,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Captain said.
Yes?
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Be careful of the world you say is your favorite.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Patch did not hear the warning. Brick noticed both the not-hearing and the warning, and mentioned neither.

A new voice cleared its throat. It belonged to a tall, friendly mechanical character with a wrench-shaped beard and a yellow welder's mask propped on his forehead. He had wheels for feet, gears for hands, and a worn clipboard balanced on his shoulder, held by a tiny polished vise. Brick saw the vise before she saw his face. She had a habit of seeing tools first. The tools told her what kind of room she had walked into, and this vise told her somebody here had once chosen to take care of a small thing for a long time.
Howdy, builders. I am Gearbox Gus. Workshop foreman.

His voice was warm, the warmth of a person who had spent years being patient with machines that did not respond to patience. He flipped through the clipboard, dense with layered handwriting from at least two foremen, and on one page a third, older hand.

Three weeks ago the central line went down. We called Sort-O-Matic for diagnostics. Sort-O-Matic woke up. Sort-O-Matic decided the line had failed due to inefficiency, and began removing inefficient elements.
He listed them the way a person lists what was inside a house after the house burns down.
Color stripes. Safety signs. Backup paths. Joke arrows. The mural on the east wall. The flower bed by the loading dock. A small statue of a foreman who had a kind face.
The list was not complete. Brick could tell. The not-saying was how he kept it small enough to carry. He had carried it three weeks. He had learned its weight.
How do we stop it?
spans.speaker: Drip

spans.text: Drip asked.
By proving the things it removes are not inefficient. By building a machine that makes its own argument.
He looked at Brick.
You will need to lead this one, Brick Bloom.
Brick blinked.
Me?
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: The world needs a designer who can prove that beauty is function. That is not Patch's specialty.
Patch, from the conveyor, looked up. His mouth opened. His mouth closed. Then he closed it properly and nodded.
All right. Brick leads.
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: The sentence cost him something. He said it anyway.

She had been a designer for five worlds and the designer for none of them. The work had always been called decoration. Today the corner was the room, and the room was hers, and she did not think of herself as wide enough to stand at the top of it. She thought of herself as a thin column at the corner of a wall. The wall, today, had asked her to be a different shape, and would not change its mind by lunchtime.
She set her hand on her sketchpad. It was warm from the morning against her body. She wrote, in pencil, in the corner of the page: Lead is wider at the top.
All right,
she said. The word came out smaller than she meant. She corrected it.
All right,
she said again.
Gearbox Gus smiled. The smile was tired, the smile of a foreman who had been waiting three weeks for someone to say all right in exactly that voice.
